text:
Help me write an open letter. I own an independent pharmacy, and I'm writing for 38 independent pharmacies in our state to the state employees' health plan. We'll send it to the plan and to the two newspapers in the capital.

Facts:
- Since January the plan pays us on average $1.80 less per prescription than it costs us to buy and fill it, for the 20 generic drugs we fill most.
- Plan members make up about 22% of the prescriptions at our 38 pharmacies.
- 9 independent pharmacies in the state closed in the last 2 years. We don't know how many closed because of rates.
- In 14 counties, the nearest pharmacy for most people is an independent one.
- The plan's contract with its pharmacy benefit manager comes up for renewal on July 1.
- My own pharmacy filled about 3,100 prescriptions for plan members last year.

I want the letter to say that a third of the independent pharmacies in the state will close within a year if nothing changes. One page.

Before I draft, five questions. The first one matters most.

1. **What is the "a third will close within a year" figure based on?** None of the facts you gave support it yet. The plan will dispute it, and the two newspapers will ask where it came from. If you have something behind it, tell me what it is. That could be a survey of the 38, or owners telling you they'll close or drop the plan by a certain date. If you don't, I'd suggest a version your facts can carry. For example, I could say how many of the 38 say they can't keep filling plan prescriptions at a loss past July 1. Or I could point to the 14 counties where the closest pharmacy is an independent one, and say what happens there if those stores go. Which way do you want to go?

2. **What exactly are you asking the plan to do?** One possibility: write a rule into the July 1 contract renewal that the plan can never pay less than a drug costs to buy and fill. Others are an emergency rate change before July, a meeting, or a public review of the contract with the pharmacy benefit manager. A single clear ask will make the letter stronger.

3. **How many independent pharmacies are there in the state?** That tells readers what share the 38 make up. It would also give a "third of them" number its real size if you keep that claim.

4. **What does the loss cost your own pharmacy?** The $1.80 average applies only to the 20 generics you fill most. Roughly how many of your 3,100 plan prescriptions were those drugs? I could also use one specific patient or town story you're comfortable having in print.

5. **Who signs, and who is it addressed to?** Do you want the plan's executive director or board named? Should it be signed by you alone "on behalf of 38 independent pharmacies," or should all 38 be listed? Listing them would take up much of the page.

1. You're right, I don't have anything behind the "a third" number. I can't name stores that will close or say how many of the 9 closed because of rates. Use what the facts support. Two of our 38 have told me they'll stop filling for plan members if nothing changes. And in those 14 counties the nearest chain pharmacy is more than 20 miles away for most people.

2. The July 1 renewal should pay at least what the drug costs us, plus a fill fee. I can also commit to sharing our purchase invoices for the 20 drugs with the plan, and to meeting with their staff any time before May 1.

3. I don't know.

4. I don't know how many of my 3,100 were those 20 drugs. I don't have a patient story ready.

5. I don't have a preference on who it's addressed to, so go with what you think. Sign it from me, Tom Reilly, owner of Reilly Drug in Carver, on behalf of the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance, 38 independent pharmacies. Don't list all 38.

I wrote the letter without the "a third will close" claim and used the two pharmacies' warning and the 20-mile gap instead.

<final_document>
**An Open Letter to the State Employees' Health Plan**

To the Board of Trustees and Executive Director:

We are the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance, 38 independent pharmacies across the state. We are writing because the plan now pays us less than it costs us to fill its members' prescriptions, and that can't continue.

Since January, the plan has paid us an average of $1.80 less than it costs us to buy and fill each prescription for the 20 generic drugs we fill most often. Each of those prescriptions loses money. Plan members make up about 22 percent of the prescriptions at our pharmacies, more than one in five. No small business can keep doing a fifth of its work at a loss.

Some of us have reached the limit. Two of our 38 pharmacies have told us they will stop filling prescriptions for plan members if nothing changes.

Here is what that means for your members. In 14 counties in this state, the nearest pharmacy for most people is an independent one. For most people in those counties, the nearest chain pharmacy is more than 20 miles away. If an independent pharmacy there stops taking the plan, your members lose the pharmacy in their own town. They will have to drive 20 miles or more for a refill.

Nine independent pharmacies in this state have closed in the past two years. We can't say how many of them closed because of rates, and we won't pretend to know. But we do know that every pharmacy still open is now losing money on its most common plan prescriptions.

The plan has a clear chance to fix this. Its contract with its pharmacy benefit manager comes up for renewal on July 1. **We ask that the renewed contract pay pharmacies at least what each drug costs us, plus a fee for filling the prescription.**

We don't expect you to take our word for the numbers. We will:

- **share our purchase invoices** for these 20 drugs with the plan, so your staff can check our costs for themselves; and
- **meet with your staff at any time before May 1**, wherever and whenever suits you.

Last year my pharmacy, Reilly Drug in Carver, filled about 3,100 prescriptions for plan members. They are teachers, road crews, office staff and retirees. We want to keep serving them. We are asking for a contract that lets us.

Sincerely,

Tom Reilly
Owner, Reilly Drug, Carver
On behalf of the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance, 38 independent pharmacies

[Contact phone / email]
</final_document>

A few things to check before you send it:

- **Who it's addressed to:** I used "Board of Trustees and Executive Director." If you can find the director's name, use it. A letter to a named person is harder to pass along without an answer.
- **Who your members are:** "Teachers, road crews, office staff and retirees" was my guess at who's in a state employees' plan. Change it if that's wrong for your state, or cut it.
- **Contact line:** I left a placeholder so the plan's staff and the reporters have a way to reach you. Fill it in or delete it.
- **Dates:** I wrote July 1 and May 1 without years. That assumes the July 1 renewal is next year's, July 2027. Add the years if there's any chance someone could misread them.
- **Length:** It's about 430 words, so it should fit on one page with a letterhead.
